title: The Sehskriti's warnings
hook: wealth, youth and family are passing, it says (Salok Sehskriti)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salok Sehskriti and their stately sound. Your line was the old tongue.

Katanch. Katanch. Katanch. The word knocks like a hand on a door, again and again. It opens one of Guru Arjan's verses in the Salok Sehskriti, and roughly it asks: where is? who is? Where is the mother, where is the father, where is the wife, the son? A question asked that many times in a row stops being a question and becomes a drumbeat. Yesterday was the old style. Today is what that style says, and it's a plain warning.
screen: `KATANCH, KATANCH, KATANCH.` → `WHERE IS? WHO IS?` → `A QUESTION BECOMES A DRUMBEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, paraphrased. Who is mother, who is father, who is wife, who are the children you delight in? Who are brother, friend and kin, and what is the pull of the household? The bright, enchanting beauty of the world: you see it, and it leaves. What stays with you, Nanak says, is the remembrance of the Lord. Put simply, these warnings name three things that pass: wealth, youth, family. Now a careful note, because this is easy to mishear. Sikh teachers don't read it as a command to walk away from family. This path has seen Guru Ram Das build a town and pass the Guruship to his son, and Sikh teaching honors the householder's life. Katanch isn't asking whether your mother matters. It's asking where she can go with you, in the end, and where you can go with her. The honest answer: not all the way. Every bond has a door it can't pass through. Some readers hear the verse less as a loss and more as a sorting. Love your people fully, it seems to say, and don't make them carry the weight only the Name can hold. If a loss is heavy on you right now, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `WHO IS MOTHER, WHO IS FATHER?` · `NOT A COMMAND TO LEAVE HOME.` · `EVERY BOND HAS A DOOR.` · `ONLY THE NAME GOES ALL THE WAY.` · then, large: `PASSING THINGS.`

segments.voice: Choose something you love that won't last forever: a cup you use every morning, a season, your own strength. Hold it in your mind, or in your hands if it's near, and loosen your grip a little, the way you'd hold a bird. Be grateful it's here and honest that it passes, and if you pray, let Waheguru ride each breath out.
The Sehskriti's warnings. Mother, father, child, the world's bright beauty: they pass, this verse says; the remembrance of the Lord stays. Today's word.
Your line: passing things. That closes a week of letters and old tongues. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: That katanch verse, where is mother, where is father: is it telling people to leave their families?
options: No. Love them fully; every bond has a door, and only the Name goes on.
Yes. The verse is a plain order to leave your home and family behind.
No. It's saying family love doesn't matter much, so don't dwell on it.
chat.meaning: Sikh teaching honors the householder. Katanch asks where your people can go with you in the end, and answers honestly: not all the way.
